findings.description: All div_ overloads and fraction() ultimately perform Solidity division without validating the denominator is non-zero. If any upstream caller can cause b (or b.mantissa) to be zero (e.g., via user input, misconfiguration, or a manipulated/zeroed value), the entire operation reverts and can DoS the calling action.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit `require(denominator != 0)` checks (or upstream validation) for all public/external code paths that can reach these helpers with attacker-influenced denominators. Consider returning a sentinel value or bubbling a controlled error if the broader system expects non-reverting behavior.
findings.title: Division by zero causes hard reverts

findings.description: Scaled math multiplies before dividing by the scale, so intermediate products can overflow even when the final scaled result would fit. In Solidity >=0.8, this triggers a hard revert; if upstream code allows attacker-influenced mantissas (or extreme parameterization), an attacker can force reverts and DoS key flows.
findings.recommendation: Use a 512-bit mulDiv-style routine (e.g., FullMath.mulDiv) for `(a*b)/scale` patterns, and/or bound mantissas/inputs in upstream public/external functions to prevent overflow-prone ranges.
findings.title: Scaled multiplications can overflow and revert

findings.description: The constructor does not validate the initial recipient address. If deployed with `account == address(0)`, the entire fixed supply is assigned to the zero address and becomes unrecoverable, permanently breaking token distribution and governance assumptions.
findings.recommendation: Add `require(account != address(0), ...)` in the constructor (or enforce non-zero in the deploying factory/script).
findings.title: Constructor allows minting supply to zero

findings.description: `delegateBySig` uses raw `ecrecover` without enforcing low-`s` / valid `v` constraints, so signatures are malleable. An attacker can transform a user’s signature into an alternative valid `(v,s)` form and front-run it, causing the user’s original transaction to revert (nonce already used) while still executing the delegation, resulting in reliable gas griefing.
findings.recommendation: Use OpenZeppelin `ECDSA.recover` (which enforces low-`s` and `v` checks) or add explicit checks for `v in {27,28}` and `s <= secp256k1n/2` before `ecrecover`.
findings.title: Malleable signatures enable delegateBySig griefing

findings.description: Checkpoint writing truncates `block.number` to `uint32` via `safe32`, which will revert once the chain exceeds `2**32 - 1` blocks. After that point, any operation that writes checkpoints (delegations/transfers affecting voting power) will fail, potentially breaking governance vote tracking permanently.
findings.recommendation: Store checkpoint `fromBlock` as `uint64/uint256` (and update `safe32`/struct types) to avoid a hard liveness cutoff.
findings.title: Vote checkpointing breaks after 2^32 blocks

findings.description: Multiple quote paths compute `10 ** decimals` from the underlying ERC20. If a listed/whitelisted asset reports an unusually large `decimals()` value, exponentiation will overflow and revert, breaking `quoteOpen`, `feePToken`, `expectedOut`, and related helpers. This can render quoting (and any onchain execution depending on these view calls) unusable for that market.
findings.recommendation: Validate and cap supported `decimals()` values (e.g., <= 18 or another strict bound) at listing time and/or in the quoter before exponentiation. Alternatively, avoid exponentiation by storing pre-validated scale factors in config/oracle for each supported asset.
findings.title: Token decimals exponentiation can brick quotes

findings.description: `flashAmountForLeverage` subtracts `LEVERAGE_SCALE` from `leverageX100` without validating the input. For `leverageX100 <= 100` this underflows and reverts, which can unexpectedly break integrations relying on this "legacy" ABI endpoint for quoting.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit `require(leverageX100 > LEVERAGE_SCALE)` (or return 0) to make the failure mode predictable and integration-safe.
findings.title: Legacy leverage quote reverts on low leverage

findings.description: The staleness check subtracts `updatedAt` from `block.timestamp` without ensuring `updatedAt <= block.timestamp`. If a feed ever returns a future `updatedAt` (misconfigured feed, L2 timestamp issues, or malicious aggregator set by admin), the subtraction underflows and reverts, breaking oracle reads and any protocol actions that depend on them.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite staleness logic to avoid subtraction underflow, e.g., `if (updatedAt <= block.timestamp && block.timestamp - updatedAt <= threshold)` or `if (updatedAt + threshold >= block.timestamp)` with safe bounds. Apply the same fix everywhere the pattern appears.
findings.title: Future updatedAt can revert price reads

findings.description: The oracle ignores `answeredInRound` and `roundId` from `latestRoundData()`. Without checking `answeredInRound >= roundId`, the contract may accept incomplete/stale round answers, returning an incorrect price that can be exploited for bad debt or unfair liquidations when the feed is mid-update or reporting lagging data.
findings.recommendation: Validate Chainlink round completeness: require `answeredInRound >= roundId` and (optionally) `updatedAt != 0`. Consider also enforcing additional sanity checks (min/max bounds if available) and using a dedicated Chainlink library pattern.
findings.title: Chainlink round completeness not validated

findings.description: If no Chainlink feed is registered (or it is stale and `lastValidChainlinkPrice` is zero) and no manual price is set, the oracle returns `0`. In Compound-style comptrollers, a zero underlying price for a listed borrow market can make borrows appear value-less, potentially allowing unlimited borrowing of that asset (or causing downstream division-by-zero/DoS in liquidation math), depending on the surrounding protocol’s validations.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed when no valid price exists: revert (or return a sentinel) if neither a fresh Chainlink price nor a nonzero manual price is available. Additionally, enforce nonzero prices at market listing time and when removing feeds.
findings.title: Zero price fallback can enable free borrowing

findings.description: `pTokenFromUnderlying` divides by `exchangeRate` without checking for zero. If a misconfigured/malicious pToken reports `exchangeRate == 0`, operations that need pToken amounts for USD targets (e.g., liquidation sizing) will revert and can block critical flows for that market.
findings.recommendation: Validate `exchangeRate != 0` before calling `mulDiv` (either in this library or at each call site) and treat zero as an invalid market state with a clear error.
findings.title: Zero exchangeRate causes division-by-zero reverts

findings.description: PToken only validates a new controller via a spoofable marker (`isPeridottroller`) rather than proving it implements the full expected Peridottroller behavior. Any attacker-controlled contract can return `true` for this marker, and if admin/governance is tricked or compromised into setting it, subsequent policy-hook calls can revert (DoS/fund lock) or behave maliciously (e.g., allowing unsafe borrows). This weak check is defined in `PeridottrollerInterface` and relied upon in `PToken._setPeridottroller` (PToken.sol:1022-1036).
findings.recommendation: Replace the marker-method check with stronger validation (e.g., codehash allowlist, governance-approved controller registry, or multi-method `staticcall` interface conformance checks using `try/catch` and requiring success) and add operational safeguards around controller upgrades (timelock, pause-on-upgrade, audits).
findings.title: Marker boolean allows spoofed controller contracts

findings.description: The owner can set `actionDelay` to an arbitrarily large value, making all future queued configuration actions effectively unexecutable for an extremely long time. If done accidentally or maliciously, this can prevent updating critical safety parameters (fees, endpoints, risk configs) and block unpausing opens, creating a protocol liveness failure.
findings.recommendation: Add a reasonable `MAX_ACTION_DELAY` and enforce `actionDelay_ <= MAX_ACTION_DELAY` in both `queueActionDelay()` and `setActionDelay()`.
findings.title: Unbounded actionDelay can permanently stall governance

findings.description: provideCoverage() lets the liquidator choose an arbitrary pToken address and transfers up to the contract’s full balance of that token to an arbitrary recipient. If the liquidator is compromised/misconfigured (or is a contract that untrusted parties can trigger), all ERC20s held by the fund (including unrelated/accidentally sent tokens) can be drained.
findings.recommendation: Restrict pToken to an allowlist of supported assets (settable by owner with events), and/or enforce recipient constraints (e.g., only known margin/liquidation modules). Consider a per-asset max payout/ratelimit to reduce blast radius of liquidator compromise.
findings.title: Liquidator can transfer any token held

findings.description: recoverUnsupportedToken() allows the owner to transfer any ERC20 (including the intended insurance/coverage assets) to an arbitrary recipient. A malicious/compromised owner can exfiltrate all funds, breaking the invariant that funds remain available for coverage.
findings.recommendation: If this is intended, document it as an explicit trust assumption and gate it behind a timelock/multisig. Otherwise, block recovery of supported assets (or cap withdrawals) and/or require a delay + on-chain announcement for recoveries.
findings.title: Owner can withdraw all insurance assets

findings.description: USD conversion relies on `10 ** assetDecimals` without bounding `assetDecimals`. If a listed underlying token reports a large (or mutable) decimals value, the exponentiation can overflow and revert, breaking metrics, liquidation quoting, and liquidation flows for that market. Even without overflow, a malicious token that changes `decimals()` after positions exist can skew collateral/debt USD values and violate leverage/health invariants.
findings.recommendation: At market listing time, snapshot and store an immutable decimals value and enforce a safe bound (e.g., `<= 18`, or at minimum `<= 77` to avoid `10**decimals` overflow). Avoid querying `decimals()` dynamically from untrusted tokens during risk-critical calculations.
findings.title: Token decimals overflow bricks USD conversions

findings.description: The protocol stores each user’s entered markets in `accountAssets`, intended to be capped by `maxAssets`, but `addToMarketInternal` never checks `accountAssets[borrower].length` against `maxAssets`. A user can enter an arbitrary number of markets, making liquidity/permission checks that iterate `accountAssets` increasingly expensive and potentially uncallable within gas limits. This can brick core actions (borrow/redeem/liquidate) for the user and can amplify gas costs for any paths that touch that account.
findings.impacted_code:
uint256 public maxAssets;
mapping(address => PToken[]) public accountAssets;
findings.recommendation: Enforce `accountAssets[borrower].length < maxAssets` in `addToMarketInternal` (and any other entry points) before pushing a new market; add regression tests for gas-growth and cap behavior.
findings.title: Missing maxAssets enforcement enables unbounded markets

findings.description: `allMarkets` is an ever-growing array, and public reward-claim helpers typically iterate over it (e.g., claim-all patterns). As markets are added, these loops can exceed block gas limits, preventing users from using the convenience claim-all function and potentially breaking integrations that rely on it. Users may be forced to claim in batches, and some UIs/keepers may fail entirely as the array grows.
findings.impacted_code:
/// @notice A list of all markets
PToken[] public allMarkets;
findings.recommendation: Provide and document bounded/batched claim functions (or require callers to pass a market subset), and avoid any mandatory iteration over `allMarkets` in critical paths.
findings.title: allMarkets growth can DoS reward claims

findings.description: The proxy uses a long inheritance chain of storage contracts without reserved storage gaps. Any future upgrade that inserts/reorders variables (or forgets to inherit the latest storage version) can corrupt critical slots such as `admin` or `peridottrollerImplementation`, potentially leading to permanent bricking or loss of control. This is an operational footgun for a delegatecall-based upgrade pattern.
findings.recommendation: Adopt an explicit storage-gap pattern (e.g., `uint256[__] private __gap;`) per version, and enforce upgrade procedures/tests that validate storage layout compatibility between Unitroller and new implementations.
findings.title: No storage gap increases upgrade collision risk

findings.description: `mintFresh` mints `mintTokens = actualMintAmount / exchangeRate` without enforcing `mintTokens > 0`. An attacker can mint a tiny amount to obtain minimal pToken supply, then directly donate underlying to the market to inflate `exchangeRate`, causing later user mints to round down to 0 pTokens (users lose their deposit while attacker’s existing pTokens capture the donated cash). The attacker can then redeem their pTokens to extract most/all donated cash, including victims’ deposits.
findings.recommendation: Revert when `mintTokens == 0` (or when `actualMintAmount` is below a protocol-defined minimum), and/or mint a small “dead” initial supply to a burn address to reduce exchange-rate manipulation. Consider explicitly rejecting markets with donation-sensitive underlying (rebasing/fee-on-transfer) and documenting minimum mint amounts in frontend/SDK.
findings.title: Mint can silently issue zero pTokens

findings.description: The constructor forwards `initialOwner` to `ProxyAdmin` without validating it is non-zero. If deployed with `address(0)`, `ProxyAdmin` ownership is irrecoverably lost, preventing any future proxy upgrades or admin operations.
findings.recommendation: Add a zero-address check in the constructor (or enforce via deployment tooling) to ensure `initialOwner != address(0)`.
findings.title: Zero owner address bricks upgrade authority

findings.description: `sweepToken` uses `EIP20NonStandardInterface(token).transfer(admin, balance)` and ignores any boolean return value for standard ERC-20s that signal failure by returning `false` instead of reverting. In that case the sweep transaction succeeds but tokens remain stuck in the contract, impairing recovery operations and potentially breaking incident response procedures.
findings.impacted_code:
uint256 balance = token.balanceOf(address(this));
token.transfer(admin, balance);
findings.recommendation: Use the same return-data checking pattern as `doTransferOut`, or use OpenZeppelin `SafeERC20` (with a low-level call) to support both standard and non-standard tokens and to revert on failure.
findings.title: Sweep can silently fail to transfer

findings.description: Unitroller allows setting/accepting an implementation address without verifying it has contract code. If admin (or a deployment script) sets an EOA/zero-code address as the implementation, subsequent calls through the fallback will delegatecall into an address with no runtime code, returning empty data and causing downstream ABI decoding failures (protocol-wide DoS).
findings.recommendation: Validate `newPendingImplementation != address(0)` and `newPendingImplementation.code.length > 0` in `_setPendingImplementation` (and/or `_acceptImplementation`). Consider also guarding fallback with an explicit check that `peridottrollerImplementation.code.length > 0` to fail fast with a clear error.
findings.title: Proxy can upgrade to non-contract address

findings.description: Borrow debt share accounting enforces `borrowIndex <= BorrowAccounting.SCALE` and reverts once the index exceeds `1e36`. Since `borrowIndex` monotonically increases and can exceed `1e36` over a multi-year horizon at sustained high borrow rates, `accrueInterest()` will start reverting, freezing core market actions (mint/redeem/borrow/repay/liquidate) that require interest accrual. This creates a time-triggered, potentially irreversible liveness failure once borrow accounting is enabled.
findings.recommendation: Remove the hard cap on `borrowIndex`, or replace it with a bound derived from actual overflow risk (e.g., rely on `Math.mulDiv`’s 512-bit safety) and/or implement periodic rescaling of shares/index to keep values in range without reverting.
findings.title: Borrow index cap can permanently brick market

findings.description: All accounts are permanently bound to a single `executor` because it can only be set once in the factory and each clone enforces `manager_ == factory.executor()` during initialization. If the executor becomes unusable (paused/buggy/upgraded to reverting logic), users may be unable to manage positions (repay/withdraw/adjust), potentially forcing liquidations or locking funds until an off-chain migration. There is no on-chain recovery path to rotate the executor for existing accounts.
findings.recommendation: Add a controlled executor-rotation mechanism (e.g., timelocked `setExecutor` update) and a corresponding account-side authorization scheme (e.g., allow factory-approved manager updates) so existing accounts can be migrated safely if the executor fails.
findings.title: Non-rotatable executor can permanently lock accounts

findings.description: The adapter enforces exact balance deltas on all transfers (`_pullExact`/`_pushExact`) and around router/position-manager interactions. Any fee-on-transfer, rebasing, ERC-777 hook side-effects, or token upgrades that change transfer behavior can cause persistent `BalanceDeltaMismatch` reverts, effectively bricking adds/swaps/withdrawals for that pair. `registerPair()` does not validate token behavior, so misconfiguration (or later token changes) can lock operations.
findings.recommendation: Explicitly restrict supported tokens (document and enforce “plain ERC-20, no fees/rebasing/hooks”), or relax accounting to tolerate known behaviors (e.g., measure received amounts instead of requiring exact deltas). Add an emergency unregister/migrate path for misconfigured pairs.
findings.title: Exact balance-delta checks can brick tokens

findings.description: The factory only checks `executor_.code.length > 0` at configuration time, but `createAccount()` does not re-validate that the stored executor is still a contract. If the executor address later becomes an EOA-like caller (e.g., via future account-code mechanisms such as EIP-7702-style delegation changes, or chain-specific code removal semantics), that key holder would directly be the `manager` for all new accounts and could call privileged `onlyManager` functions to move assets.
findings.recommendation: In `createAccount()`, add `require(executor.code.length > 0, ...)` (and consider pinning executor bytecode hash / using an immutable executor) to ensure the manager remains a contract with expected behavior.
findings.title: Executor contractness not enforced after configuration

findings.description: `liquidationRedeem()` lets the current `riskEngine.liquidator()` redeem collateral and transfer underlying to an arbitrary recipient, without verifying the account is actually in liquidation. Because the controller/risk-engine movement gate typically short-circuits when `borrowBalanceStored(account)==0`, a compromised/malicious liquidator can steal collateral from accounts that have repaid debt but still hold pTokens. This turns the liquidator role into a blanket withdrawal key for debt-free accounts’ collateral.
findings.recommendation: Bind `liquidationRedeem()` to an on-chain liquidation state/authorization: require the risk engine reports this account is in `LIQUIDATING` status and enforce a same-block, amount-bounded movement authorization even when debt is zero (e.g., add a dedicated `consumeLiquidationMovement(account,pToken,amount)` hook in the risk engine/controller and require it here). Also consider restricting `recipient` to a whitelisted liquidation module rather than arbitrary addresses.
findings.title: Liquidator can redeem debt-free collateral anytime

findings.description: The vault assumes `safeTransferFrom(receiver, this, amount + fee)` increases its balance by exactly `amount + fee`, but this is false for fee-on-transfer/rebasing/deflationary tokens. An attacker can repeatedly flash-loan such a token and repay the nominal `amount + fee` while the vault receives less each time, causing gradual loss of principal. The only guard is `tokenAllowed`, so if a non-standard token is mistakenly allowed, funds can be drained.
findings.recommendation: Only allow well-behaved ERC20s (no transfer fees/rebases) and/or enforce balance-delta checks (record pre/post balances and require `postBalance >= preBalance + fee`, or require exact repayment for `amount`).
findings.title: Fee-on-transfer tokens drain vault over time

findings.description: `depositLiquidity` is callable by any address, but there is no accounting to let depositors withdraw their funds; only `onlyOwner` can withdraw arbitrary tokens to an arbitrary recipient. Any user who deposits (intentionally or by mistake) can have funds permanently locked or effectively donated to the owner, violating typical vault expectations.
findings.recommendation: Either restrict `depositLiquidity` to `onlyOwner`/authorized actors, or implement depositor share accounting with permissionless withdrawals to the depositor.
findings.title: Anyone can deposit but only owner withdraws

findings.description: When `paused == true`, `maxFlashLoan` correctly returns 0, but `flashFee` still returns a fee (it only checks `tokenAllowed`). Integrations that pre-quote fees via `flashFee` can be misled into submitting flash loan transactions that will always revert due to `require(!paused)` in `flashLoan`.
findings.recommendation: Make `flashFee` return 0 or revert when paused (matching `maxFlashLoan`/`flashLoan` behavior) to avoid inconsistent interface responses.
findings.title: flashFee ignores paused state causing integration grief

findings.description: _setImplementation() assigns the new implementation without validating it is a real contract and not address(0) or this contract. If admin mistakenly sets an EOA/zero address, all delegated calls will revert (locking user funds). If set to address(this), the fallback/dispatch path can recurse until out-of-gas, permanently DoSing core actions (mint/redeem/repay/borrow).
findings.recommendation: In _setImplementation, require implementation_ != address(0) && implementation_ != address(this) and extcodesize(implementation_) > 0 (or Address.isContract). Consider emitting an explicit failure event if validation fails.
findings.title: Invalid implementation address can brick markets

findings.description: The contract rejects ETH sent through the fallback and provides no method to recover ETH accidentally or forcibly sent via SELFDESTRUCT. As a result, any ETH force-fed to the delegator becomes unrecoverable, creating dust balances and complicating accounting/monitoring.
findings.recommendation: Add an admin-only ETH sweep function (or a receive() that wraps ETH into WETH if desired) to allow recovering force-sent ETH.
findings.title: Forced ETH can become permanently stuck

findings.description: The owner can replace the price source and arbitrarily change/delist market registrations, which directly affects margin valuations used for liquidation and account health checks. A compromised/malicious owner (or governance capture) can set an asset source that returns manipulated prices or deregister markets to make positions unpriceable, leading to wrongful liquidations or protocol-wide liveness failures for affected accounts.
findings.recommendation: Constrain governance risk with a timelock + on-chain delay for `setAssetSource`/market changes, add an emergency pause scoped to new actions (not withdrawals), and consider immutable or bounded/whitelisted price sources. Emit and monitor these events with automated alerts.
findings.title: Admin can swap oracle and misprice

findings.description: The “fail-closed” boosted-market protection (returning zero asset when the vault claim is unreadable) is only applied when `isBoostedMarket[pToken]` is true. The owner can (accidentally or maliciously) re-register a boosted market with `boosted=false`, disabling the readability check and reintroducing the collateral undervaluation/liquidation risk the contract is meant to prevent when the vault claim read fails inside the pToken’s exchange-rate logic.
findings.recommendation: Make `boosted` a one-way flag (cannot be turned off once enabled), or require an explicit safety review process (timelock + guardian veto) before toggling it. Consider validating boosted-ness from the market itself (or storing immutable market metadata) rather than trusting a mutable flag.
findings.title: Boosted-market safety can be disabled by owner

findings.description: `PTokenStorage` appends new flash-loan state variables, changing the storage layout for all inheritors (e.g., `PErc20Storage.underlying` and `CDelegationStorage.implementation`). If an existing `PErc20Delegator` (deployed with the old layout) is upgraded to an implementation compiled against this new layout, the implementation will read/write critical fields from the wrong slots (e.g., treating an empty slot as `underlying`), breaking core mint/redeem/borrow flows and potentially bricking markets permanently.
findings.recommendation: Do not change the storage layout used by existing delegator/proxy deployments. Either (1) deploy new markets with the new layout, (2) add new variables only in an unused reserved storage gap that already exists in the old layout, or (3) perform an explicit storage migration via a new delegator/proxy that matches the updated layout (with user fund migration). Also add a documented storage-gap pattern for future upgrades.
findings.title: Upgrading proxy breaks storage slot alignment

findings.description: `onFlashLoan` performs multiple external calls but is not protected by `nonReentrant`, while `liquidate` is callable during the flash-loan callback. A reentrant call into `liquidate` can overwrite `_pending` mid-callback, breaking the invariant that one liquidation is processed at a time and potentially causing incorrect accounting (repay/approvals/rewards) or stuck/reverted liquidations depending on token/router behavior. This becomes exploitable if any called external contract/token can trigger a callback into this contract (e.g., malicious flash lender/router/underlying token or an upgrade/change in those dependencies).
findings.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` (or an equivalent single-flight mutex) to `onFlashLoan`, and/or add an explicit `require(!_pending.active && _pending.positionId==0)` style guard in `liquidate` to prevent nested liquidations during a callback.
findings.title: Reentrant liquidations can overwrite pending state

findings.description: `initialize` has no access control beyond `initializer`, so any account can initialize a freshly deployed proxy if the deployer forgets to atomically initialize it. An attacker can set `executor/config/riskEngine/vault/insuranceFund/quoter/swapModule` to malicious contracts and then steal funds during liquidations or permanently brick the system. This is a common upgradeable-deployment footgun with concrete loss potential when proxies are deployed uninitialized.
findings.recommendation: Ensure proxies are always deployed with an atomic initialization call (e.g., via constructor calldata in the proxy). Optionally add an access control check in `initialize` (e.g., `onlyOwner`/`onlyAdmin`) or use OpenZeppelin's `TransparentUpgradeableProxy` pattern with admin-controlled initialization.
findings.title: Initializer can be front-run on proxies

findings.description: The flash-repayment solvency check computes `available = balanceOf(this) - baseDebtBalance`, assuming the debt asset's balance only changes by explicit transfers/swaps in this transaction. If the debt asset is rebasing/fee-on-transfer (or otherwise changes balance independently), `available` can be miscomputed, causing false reverts (DoS) or incorrect surplus calculation impacting liquidator rewards and returned margin. This risk is amplified because the code also relies on exact-balance deltas in swap/mint/redeem flows.
findings.recommendation: Restrict supported underlying assets to non-rebasing, non-fee-on-transfer ERC20s and enforce this at market listing time, or compute deltas using internal accounting of actual proceeds (e.g., track pre/post balances around each operation) instead of a single `baseDebtBalance` snapshot.
findings.title: Available-balance math breaks on rebasing tokens

findings.description: Most state transitions (activateAccount/beginClose/finishClose/beginLiquidation/finishLiquidation) rely on _metrics(), which reverts when oracle.marketAsset() is zero or oracle.getPrice() returns 0. If the oracle returns 0 due to staleness, misconfiguration, or a boosted market vault-claim read failure, all critical operations (including liquidations) can be blocked, potentially trapping funds and delaying bad-debt resolution.
findings.recommendation: Add a controlled fallback path for price unavailability (e.g., allow liquidation/close using conservative haircuts or last-known-good prices with staleness bounds), and/or store and validate oracle staleness/heartbeat so prices fail deterministically before positions are opened.
findings.title: Oracle outage can freeze close/liquidation flows

findings.description: finishClose() and finishLiquidation() attempt to ensure the action improved the account by comparing against a caller-supplied previousHealthFactorBps. Because this value is not stored when beginClose()/beginLiquidation() is called, the executor/liquidator can pass any value (e.g., 0) and bypass the intended invariant, potentially restoring ACTIVE status after a close/liquidation attempt that did not actually improve safety.
findings.recommendation: Store the previous health factor (or a hash of relevant state) in contract storage during beginClose()/beginLiquidation(), and validate it in finishClose()/finishLiquidation(). Alternatively, remove the parameter and recompute the pre-state from stored snapshots if feasible.
findings.title: Unstored health factor allows bypassing checks

findings.description: _consumeMovement() unconditionally allows any redeem/transfer when borrowBalanceStored() is zero, regardless of account status or movement authorization. If other system components assume collateral movement is always mediated by authorizeMovement() while a position exists, this can allow unmediated collateral withdrawals whenever the stored debt reaches 0 (including during OPENING/ACTIVE) and may break higher-level state machine assumptions.
findings.recommendation: Gate the debt==0 fast-path by account status (e.g., only allow unrestricted movement when status is CLOSED/LIQUIDATED), or require an explicit close path (beginDebtFreeClose/finishClose) before allowing collateral movement without authorization.
findings.title: Movement bypassed when stored debt equals zero

findings.description: This wrapper’s constructor parameter `admin_` is forwarded as `initialOwner` to OpenZeppelin v5’s `TransparentUpgradeableProxy`, which deploys a new `ProxyAdmin` owned by `initialOwner` (not set as the proxy admin itself). If deployers mistakenly pass an existing ProxyAdmin address (thinking it is the proxy admin), the newly created ProxyAdmin will be owned by that contract address, making `onlyOwner` upgrades effectively impossible and permanently locking upgradeability.
findings.recommendation: Rename `admin_` to `initialOwner` and document OZ v5 semantics clearly in deployment scripts. Add deployment-time assertions/tests to prevent passing a ProxyAdmin address as `initialOwner` (or explicitly accept a ProxyAdmin instance rather than creating a new one).
findings.title: Misnamed admin argument can brick upgrades

findings.description: executeSwap() always reads the router adapter from config.routerAdapter() and hard-reverts when it is unset or not a contract, which halts all swap-dependent open/close/liquidation flows that call into this module. Since the config owner can update or even disable execution endpoints, a compromised or malicious owner (or a misconfiguration) can cause a system-wide DoS and potentially prevent timely liquidations, leading to bad debt.
findings.recommendation: Protect execution-endpoint changes with a robust timelock and emergency procedures (e.g., staged/dual control), and consider a fallback/allowlist of adapters or an emergency adapter to preserve liquidation ability when endpoints are disabled.
findings.title: Admin can brick swaps by disabling adapter

findings.description: When minAmountOut is zero (or set loosely), the module derives the enforceable minimum output solely from oracle pricing (expectedOut) and a configurable slippage BPS. An MEV searcher can sandwich the underlying DEX route inside the allowed oracle/slippage window to extract value from the caller (executor/liquidator), especially during volatile markets where oracle prices lag on-chain liquidity.
findings.recommendation: Always pass a DEX-quote-based minAmountOut from the caller (or enforce one in the module), and keep maxSlippageBps tight; consider using TWAP-aware quoting or integrating a route-specific quoter to bound sandwich profit.
findings.title: Sandwichable swaps when relying on oracle minOut

findings.description: executeSwap() does not validate maxSlippageBps and oracleDeviationBps are <= 10,000. Passing values above BPS causes an underflow in (BPS - parameter) and reverts, which can create unexpected failures for integrators and reduces debuggability (generic arithmetic revert instead of SwapError).
findings.recommendation: Explicitly require maxSlippageBps <= BPS and oracleDeviationBps <= BPS (and potentially cap them to risk-configured maxima) and revert with a dedicated error code.
findings.title: Missing bounds checks for slippage parameters

findings.description: Debt migration via `activate()` requires a single transaction that iterates over a complete, strictly-sorted list of every active borrower. An attacker can create a very large number of tiny borrows across many addresses right before migration, making the admin’s migration transaction exceed block gas limits and preventing activation (and therefore any upgrade path that depends on it).
findings.recommendation: Make migration chunkable (e.g., multi-tx batching with a running totalShares accumulator), or support an on-chain iterable borrower set (or a Merkle-based proof approach) so activation cannot be gas-DoS’d by borrower count.
findings.title: Borrower sybil can permanently block migration

findings.description: `assetPrices` returns 0 unless the lending oracle price exactly equals the guard’s price, causing a fail-closed price unavailability on any benign drift (different rounding, feed decimals, or update timing). If downstream margin actions revert on `PriceUnavailable`, users can be DoSed from opening/closing/repaying positions; if any path treats 0 as a real price, collateral could be misvalued. This can be triggered without compromising either oracle, simply by inducing transient disagreement between the two sources (e.g., one updates earlier in the block than the other).
findings.recommendation: Compare within a configurable tolerance (bps or absolute), or accept the guard price whenever it is valid and ensure the lending oracle is only used for staleness/paused checks. Emit/monitor an explicit disagreement signal so operations can respond safely.
findings.title: Strict price equality can zero prices

findings.description: For any `asset` other than the configured `stock` or `usd`, `assetPrices` returns 0 rather than reverting. If this price source is accidentally reused for additional markets, or if a market is misregistered to use an unsupported asset, the system will fail closed with `PriceUnavailable` and may unexpectedly block risk checks and user actions.
findings.recommendation: Consider reverting on unsupported assets (or exposing a `supportsAsset` view) to make misconfiguration detectable. Ensure deployment scripts and monitoring validate that only `stock`/`usd` are ever queried/registered.
findings.title: Non-stock assets silently priced as zero

findings.description: `cover()` computes `maxTokensByValue` using floor rounding, then computes `coveredValueUSDG` using ceil rounding and hard-reverts if `coveredValueUSDG > maxValue`. For some inputs, the floored token amount can still produce a ceiled USDG value that exceeds `maxValue` by 1 wei, reverting the entire cover operation instead of partially covering. This can create a liveness failure where the vault cannot draw from the reserve during deficit events unless it implements additional retry/adjustment logic.
findings.recommendation: Avoid reverting on this rounding edge: compute `covered` from `maxValue` using consistent rounding (e.g., derive `covered` from a ceil-safe formula), or if `coveredValueUSDG > maxValue`, decrement `covered` until it fits and proceed.
findings.title: Rounding mismatch can revert coverage calls

findings.description: `deposit()` and `_pushExact()` enforce exact pre/post `balanceOf` deltas for both sender and receiver. Any fee-on-transfer, rebasing, reflection, or otherwise non-standard ERC20 behavior (or future token upgrade) will cause these functions to revert, potentially preventing funding, coverage payouts, and admin withdrawals for an affected configured token/pair.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) explicitly restrict supported tokens at configuration time (document/enforce “no fee-on-transfer/rebasing” invariants), or (b) relax checks to only validate the contract’s received/sent amount (using balance diffs for this contract only) and handle non-standard tokens safely.
findings.title: Exact balance-delta checks can brick tokens

findings.description: When `totalSupply == 0`, the exchange rate is fixed to `initialExchangeRateMantissa` and ignores any underlying already sitting in the contract. If underlying tokens are force-fed/accidentally transferred to the market before the first mint, the first minter receives pTokens priced as if that cash didn’t exist, then can redeem to extract the pre-existing underlying balance. This can steal any underlying sent to the market before the first mint and misprice initial shares.
findings.recommendation: On first mint, incorporate existing cash into pricing (e.g., set exchange rate based on `getCashPrior()` when `totalSupply == 0`, or mint offsetting pTokens to an irrecoverable address), and/or provide an admin sweep/recovery path for accidentally transferred underlying before first mint.
findings.title: First minter can seize donated underlying

findings.description: `_setPendingAdmin` allows setting `pendingAdmin` to `address(0)`. This makes admin handover impossible via `_acceptAdmin` (which rejects `address(0)`), potentially causing operational delays and forcing the current admin to intervene to correct the state.
findings.recommendation: Add a non-zero address check in `_setPendingAdmin` (and consider emitting/using explicit errors instead of silent misconfiguration).
findings.title: Pending admin can be set to zero

findings.description: Depositor fees are streamed by setting `rewardRate = streamBudget / streamDuration`, with any remainder immediately added to `immediateReward`. When `streamBudget < streamDuration` (notably plausible for low-decimal tokens like 6 decimals), `rewardRate` becomes 0 and the entire `streamBudget` is paid immediately, defeating the intended streaming/anti-sniping behavior. An attacker can force more immediate distribution by splitting fees into small enough chunks.
findings.recommendation: Enforce a minimum `rewardRate` (or minimum `streamBudget`) for streaming, or carry forward undistributed budget instead of converting all sub-`streamDuration` amounts into immediate rewards (e.g., accumulate dust until it can be streamed).
findings.title: Small fees bypass reward streaming entirely

findings.description: `collectFee()` trusts external `config` values for fee splits and recipients; any revert or invalid return values can revert fee collection. Since the vault’s `lockForPosition()` calls `feeDistributor.collectFee()` for opening fees, a broken/malicious config (or an upgrade/misconfiguration) can halt position opens and other flows that require fee collection. This creates a concrete liveness/DoS risk controlled by the config’s upgrade/admin surface.
findings.recommendation: Add defensive handling around config reads (e.g., `try/catch` with safe defaults or explicit bounds checks), and/or enforce immutable/upgrade-safe config invariants (including BPS consistency and non-reverting getters). Consider validating config addresses and critical return values during `setVault`/initialization or via a health-check function used by keepers.
findings.title: Config misbehavior can brick fee collection

findings.description: Reward math multiplies `rewardRate` by time deltas in multiple places using checked arithmetic. If `rewardRate` is ever made extremely large (e.g., via a misbehaving token with huge amounts or a compromised/whitelisted fee collector feeding unrealistic amounts), `(periodFinish - now) * rewardRate` or `(dt) * rewardRate` can overflow and revert. Once overflowed, core paths like `_updatePool()`/`_checkpoint()` revert, preventing share updates and claims for that pool.
findings.recommendation: Use `Math.mulDiv` for time*rate calculations (or cap `rewardRate` at a safe maximum), and consider sanity limits on `amount` accepted in `collectFee()` per token/pool.
findings.title: Extreme rewards may overflow and DoS

findings.description: _settlementSwap divides by (BPS - config.maxSwapSlippageBps) when grossing up the required counter-asset. If maxSwapSlippageBps is ever set to 10,000 (or higher via an unchecked cast elsewhere), the denominator becomes zero and any withdrawal that reaches settlement will revert, potentially freezing exits for the pair.
findings.impacted_code:
counterNeeded =
    Math.mulDiv(counterNeeded, BPS, BPS - config.maxSwapSlippageBps, Math.Rounding.Ceil);
findings.recommendation: Validate config.maxSwapSlippageBps < BPS at pair registration and risk updates (and ideally enforce an upper bound well below 10,000). Add an explicit require in SettlementLib before the mulDiv as a defensive check.
findings.title: Max slippage at 100% reverts withdraw

findings.description: Settlement relies on strict balance-delta equality for reserve covers and swaps. If either token is fee-on-transfer, rebasing, blacklisting, or otherwise causes balance changes to differ from the adapter/reserve’s reported amounts, the library reverts, blocking withdrawals that require settlement and potentially locking funds.
findings.recommendation: Restrict supported tokens to non-rebasing, non-fee, non-callback ERC20s at pair registration. Alternatively, loosen invariants to tolerate known behaviors (e.g., accept >= min received) and track actual deltas rather than requiring equality.
findings.title: Exact balance delta checks can freeze tokens

findings.description: The admin can set `oracle` to the zero address or an EOA, which will make subsequent `oracle.getUnderlyingPrice(...)` calls revert due to ABI decoding on an address without code. This can brick core flows that depend on prices (borrows, redeems, liquidations, liquidity checks), potentially locking user positions until fixed.
findings.recommendation: Validate `newOracle` is non-zero and has code (`newOracle.code.length > 0`), and consider a sanity check call (e.g., `getUnderlyingPrice` on a known market) before accepting the update.
findings.title: Oracle can be set to non-contract address

findings.description: There is no enforcement of the controller's `maxAssets` limit when entering markets, allowing an account to join an unbounded number of listed markets. Since liquidation and borrow/redeem checks iterate over `accountAssets[account]`, an attacker can inflate this array (given enough listed markets) so these checks run out of gas and revert, preventing liquidation and enabling uncollectable bad debt.
findings.recommendation: Enforce a hard cap in `addToMarketInternal` (e.g., `require(accountAssets[borrower].length < maxAssets, ...)`) and ensure `maxAssets` is set to a safe value; alternatively, redesign liquidity checks to avoid iterating over an unbounded user-controlled list.
findings.title: Users can bloat markets list to block liquidation

findings.description: Although min/max bounds are defined for `closeFactorMantissa`, the admin setter does not enforce them, and `liquidationIncentiveMantissa` is also set without any bounds. Misconfiguration (or admin compromise) can disable liquidations (e.g., close factor = 0), make accounts liquidatable too aggressively, or cause arithmetic overflows in liquidation math, leading to liveness failures and potential insolvency.
findings.recommendation: Enforce sane bounds in `_setCloseFactor` and `_setLiquidationIncentive` (and emit failures on invalid values), e.g., `closeFactorMinMantissa <= new <= closeFactorMaxMantissa` and reasonable liquidation incentive limits.
findings.title: Liquidation parameters lack safety bounds enforcement

findings.description: _depositToVault assumes the vault will always accept and report exactly the requested amount. If the vault ever succeeds while returning a smaller `deposited` (capacity/rounding) or the underlying is fee-on-transfer, this function reverts inside the `try` block, bubbling up and reverting any flow that triggers `_rebalanceVault` (e.g., mint/repay/borrow/redeem via doTransferIn/doTransferOut). This can halt normal market operation even without an explicit vault revert.
findings.recommendation: Treat partial deposits as non-fatal: accept `deposited <= amount` and reconcile using actual balance deltas, or require the vault to revert on partial fills and enforce it with an explicit interface/spec + pre-deploy invariant tests. Consider skipping deposits when `deposited != amount` and emitting an event rather than reverting.
findings.title: Partial vault deposits can revert user actions

findings.description: _withdrawFromVault hard-depends on `robinhoodVault.accountedAssets` succeeding; if that view call reverts (oracle/guard issues, vault bug), withdrawals are skipped entirely. Since both operator withdrawals (syncVault/pause) and user liquidity preparation (_prepareFixedLiquidity) rely on _withdrawFromVault, prolonged view failures can make the market illiquid and prevent redemptions/borrows from accessing vault-held funds.
findings.recommendation: Add an emergency withdrawal path that attempts `withdrawForSide` without first calling `accountedAssets` (e.g., request the passed amount directly, or allow requesting type(uint256).max and let the vault clamp). Alternatively, fall back to `withdrawableAssets/liquidAssets` for clamping when `accountedAssets` fails, or allow operator-only override of the clamp.
findings.title: Vault withdrawals depend on accountedAssets view

findings.description: `actionDelay` is applied only at queue time; already-queued actions keep their original `executeAfter`. Admin can queue an action under a shorter delay, then later increase `actionDelay`, and still execute the previously queued action earlier than observers might assume based on the new delay.
findings.recommendation: If the intended invariant is “all pending actions must respect the latest delay”, store both `queuedAt` and delay-at-queue or recompute `executeAfter` based on current `actionDelay` at execution time. At minimum, document that delay is snapshotted at queue time for monitoring/ops.
findings.title: Increasing actionDelay doesn't affect queued actions

findings.description: The canary funding step requires the flash vault’s USD and STOCK balances to be exactly zero before depositing seed liquidity. Any third party can transfer either ERC20 directly to the flash vault address, making these balance checks fail and preventing this deployment flow from completing as written. This creates an operational DoS vector against the scripted migration/activation sequence.
findings.recommendation: Do not gate funding/activation on raw ERC20 balances being zero. Track deposits via internal accounting (or allow nonzero balances and fund the delta), and/or add a recovery path to sweep/ignore unsolicited transfers.
findings.title: Force-fed tokens can block canary funding

findings.description: The deployment helper uses the PeridotTransparentProxy from peridot-contracts, which is a thin wrapper over OpenZeppelin’s TransparentUpgradeableProxy and does not validate that the implementation was actually initialized. If any of the deployed upgradeable implementations has a faulty/missing initializer guard (or an initializer that does not set the expected initialized flag), the proxy could be left in an uninitialized state, allowing anyone to call initialize and seize privileged roles.
findings.recommendation: Use a proxy constructor that enforces initialization (e.g., validate the initialized flag/critical role assignments post-deploy), and ensure every upgradeable implementation uses OpenZeppelin Initializable with proper initializer/onlyInitializing modifiers. Consider deploying via a factory that performs post-deploy invariant checks (owner/admin/operator set as expected).
findings.title: Proxy lacks initialization-state validation guard

findings.description: The `executor` can arbitrarily choose `user`, `positionId`, and an attacker-controlled `account` in `lockForPosition`, pulling from any user’s `freeBalance` and transferring `marginAmount` to that account. The same executor can then call `releaseFromPosition` with `returnedAmount = 0` to delete the lock, leaving tokens in the attacker-controlled `account` while the vault’s accounting marks the user as having lost funds. If `executor` (or the `owner` that sets it) is compromised/malicious, all user deposits for allowed pTokens are stealable.
findings.recommendation: Minimize trust in `executor`: restrict `account` to a vetted factory/registry and bind it to `(user, positionId)` (or validate via an on-chain account contract that enforces ownership). Put `setExecutor` behind a timelock/multisig and consider adding an emergency pause that blocks new locks while still allowing withdrawals.
findings.title: Executor can drain user free balances

findings.description: `deposit`, `withdraw`, and position-management paths all call `_settle`, which performs an external call to `feeDistributor.claimFor`. If the fee distributor is misconfigured, upgraded incorrectly, or becomes unable to transfer rewards for a pToken, `_settle` will revert and users may be unable to withdraw or move their balances even though their principal is in the vault. This creates a liveness/fund-access dependency on the fee distributor’s correctness and token transferability.
findings.recommendation: Decouple reward claiming from core vault actions: allow `withdraw`/position updates to proceed even if reward settlement fails (e.g., wrap `claimFor` in `try/catch` and skip settlement on failure), or add an emergency mode to bypass `_settle` while freezing share updates.
findings.title: Withdrawals can be blocked by distributor failure

findings.description: When `openingFee > 0`, `lockForPosition` calls `feeDistributor.collectFee` from the vault address. In the fee distributor, `collectFee` is restricted to `feeCollectors[msg.sender]`, so position opening with fees will revert unless the vault is explicitly configured as an allowed fee collector. This hidden coupling can halt position creation unexpectedly after deployment/upgrade or configuration drift.
findings.recommendation: Enforce/verify configuration in `initialize` or via a one-time setup function (e.g., check `feeDistributor.feeCollectors(address(this))` before allowing `openingFee > 0`). Alternatively, redesign so fee collection is performed by a dedicated collector address that is set once and validated.
findings.title: Opening fee collection depends on extra configuration

findings.description: `decreaseLiquidity()` computes strict `amount0Min/amount1Min` from an oracle-derived `referenceSqrtPriceX96`, then enforces those minimums against the *current* pool execution price. An attacker can front-run the vault’s `decreaseLiquidity()` with a swap that moves the pool price beyond `removalToleranceBps`, causing the position burn/decrease to revert and preventing timely withdrawals/rebalances. This can be repeated (or sustained cheaply in low-liquidity pools) to create a liveness/DoS condition for vault operations.
findings.recommendation: Base withdrawal minimums on an execution-resilient price (e.g., TWAP) or allow an alternate emergency withdrawal path that uses current price-derived mins while accounting for IL separately. Consider widening/auto-adjusting tolerance under stress and/or using a commit-reveal or private transaction flow for vault liquidity changes.
findings.title: MEV can block liquidity withdrawals repeatedly

findings.description: The adapter computes outputs using balance deltas and only transfers `amountOut` plus any unspent input back to `fromAccount`, but it never sweeps or provides an admin recovery path for any pre-existing balances. Any ERC20 tokens accidentally or maliciously transferred to the adapter address will remain trapped indefinitely, despite the comment claiming it “never retains balances”. This can create unrecoverable funds and operational issues if tokens are dusted to the adapter.
findings.recommendation: Add an owner-only `sweep(token, to, amount)` (or equivalent) recovery function, or explicitly transfer the full `outToken` balance above `outStart` and document donation behavior; consider rejecting non-zero starting balances if invariants require zero balances.
findings.title: Force-fed token balances become permanently stuck

findings.description: A caller-supplied `deadline` is decoded as `uint256` for the router, but is down-cast to `uint48` when setting Permit2 expiration. If `deadline` exceeds `type(uint48).max`, the Permit2 expiration silently truncates, likely becoming an already-expired timestamp, causing swaps to revert unexpectedly even though the router deadline is still valid. This enables easy griefing/DoS in any upstream flow that forwards user-provided `data` deadlines.
findings.recommendation: Validate `deadline <= type(uint48).max` (and optionally `deadline >= block.timestamp`) when decoding `data`, or store/accept only `uint48` deadlines to keep router/Permit2 semantics aligned.
findings.title: Deadline truncation can unexpectedly break Permit2

findings.description: `swap()` is gated by `onlyOperator`, which requires `msg.sender` to be `manager` or an allowed operator. Since `manager` defaults to the zero address and `setManager` does not prevent setting `manager` to `address(0)`, a misconfiguration (or accidental reset) can brick all swapping functionality until corrected by the owner. This is a liveness/availability failure mode for any system relying on this adapter.
findings.recommendation: Require `manager_ != address(0)` (and optionally `manager_.code.length != 0` if it must be a contract). Consider an explicit one-time initialization flow or emitting an alert if `manager` is cleared.
findings.title: Unset manager/operators can permanently disable swaps

findings.description: Pool validation uses the current Uniswap v4 slot0 tick (spot price) and hard-reverts when deviation exceeds a bound. An attacker can temporarily push the pool price out of bounds just before (and restore after) user/keeper transactions to reliably make `validatePoolPrice`/`validateRemovalPrice` revert, censoring rebalances and (more importantly) withdrawals that depend on this check. This is most feasible when pool liquidity is thin, exactly when the guard is expected to protect operations.
findings.recommendation: Avoid using a manipulable spot tick as a hard gate for liveness-critical flows: use a TWAP/median tick over a lookback window, or redesign withdrawal paths to rely on oracle-anchored amount floors (with explicit slippage limits) without reverting solely on spot deviation. If keeping this check, consider making it soft-fail (pause/queue) rather than revert for withdrawals.
findings.title: Spot-tick check enables sandwichable withdrawal DoS

findings.description: `MAX_REMOVAL_DEVIATION_BPS` is enforced only when `maxRemovalDeviationBps != 0`, but `_removalBound()` falls back to `maxPriceDeviationBps` when it is zero. This allows configuring an effective removal bound above `MAX_REMOVAL_DEVIATION_BPS` by setting `maxRemovalDeviationBps = 0` and choosing a large `maxPriceDeviationBps`, undermining the intended upper limit on exit-price deviation.
findings.recommendation: Enforce the same maximum on the effective removal bound regardless of whether it comes from `maxRemovalDeviationBps` or the fallback (e.g., validate `maxPriceDeviationBps <= MAX_REMOVAL_DEVIATION_BPS` when `maxRemovalDeviationBps == 0`, or cap `_removalBound()` at `MAX_REMOVAL_DEVIATION_BPS`).
findings.title: Removal deviation cap bypassed via fallback bound

findings.description: Withdrawals may hard-revert when a deficit triggers a settlement swap but the pool is within the oracle removal deviation while still outside `maxSwapSlippageBps`, causing the adapter swap to revert on `minOut`. This can be induced by moving the pool price to a value that passes `validateRemovalPrice` but fails the swap’s `amountOutMinimum`, blocking withdrawals until governance/guardian intervention (e.g., pausing swaps).
findings.recommendation: Enforce at configuration time that `oracleGuard.maxRemovalDeviationBps(pairId) <= config.maxSwapSlippageBps` (or otherwise ensure the swap path cannot revert, e.g., catch swap failures and proceed with swaps paused / loss recognition).
findings.title: Withdrawal can revert from slippage mismatch

findings.description: When a withdrawal deficit triggers `SettlementLib` swaps, the trade size and `minOut` are predictable from mempool-visible state and constrained only by `maxSettlementSwapUSDG` and `maxSwapSlippageBps`. An MEV searcher can front-run to push the pool price to the worst value that still passes `validateRemovalPrice` and satisfies `minOut`, then back-run to restore price, extracting value from the vault on each settlement swap.
findings.recommendation: Route settlement swaps through private/MEV-protected execution (e.g., keeper-only or trusted relayer), reduce `maxSwapSlippageBps`/`maxSettlementSwapUSDG`, and/or use TWAP-based execution constraints that reduce manipulability at the moment of execution.
findings.title: Settlement swaps are sandwichable within bounds

findings.description: The vault enforces exact balance deltas on transfers and adapter interactions, reverting on any unexpected balance change. If configured with rebasing tokens, tokens with transfer side-effects, or tokens whose balances can change asynchronously, core flows (deposit, fee processing, withdrawals) can revert and effectively freeze assets. This restriction is not explicitly validated beyond a fee-on-transfer check on deposit.
findings.recommendation: Explicitly restrict supported assets to non-rebasing, no-hook ERC20s (document and enforce via allowlist), or relax balance-delta invariants to tolerate known-safe balance changes while still protecting against fee-on-transfer behavior.
findings.title: Strict balance-delta checks can lock funds

findings.description: The flash-loan callback accepts the lender-supplied `fee` without verifying it matches `flashFee(token, amount)`. If the configured lender is malicious or compromised, it can overstate the fee, causing the executor to borrow extra from the debt market and approve/repay an inflated amount, directly transferring excess funds to the lender.
findings.recommendation: In `onFlashLoan`, compute `expectedFee = _lender().flashFee(token, amount)` and require `fee == expectedFee` (or `fee <= expectedFee` only if the lender can legitimately discount). Consider also hard-capping `fee` via config risk parameters.
findings.title: Flash fee not validated against lender quote

findings.description: Closing fees are capped to the amount of margin pTokens produced/available for return, which can be zero during an underwater partial close. Users can reduce or eliminate closing fees by structuring closes that realize losses (or route swaps) so that no margin pTokens are minted, even though the protocol intended to charge fees based on closed notional.
findings.recommendation: If fees must always be charged on notional, collect them from remaining collateral (e.g., seize additional position pTokens for the fee) rather than capping to returned margin pTokens. Alternatively, document the intended behavior explicitly as “fees only charged on returned equity.”
findings.title: Close may undercharge fees on losses

findings.description: The swap module measures `amountOut` using its own tokenOut balance delta, then transfers exactly `amountOut` to the caller. For fee-on-transfer/rebasing `tokenOut`, the caller will receive less than `amountOut`, breaking the executor’s assumptions and potentially causing unexpected reverts or user-facing DoS for pairs using such assets.
findings.recommendation: Explicitly disallow fee-on-transfer/rebasing assets as swap outputs (and document it), or measure the caller’s received balance change instead of the module’s internal delta. Add allowlists for supported underlying tokens if needed.
findings.title: Swap module mishandles fee-on-transfer outputs
